#### **Introduction** 

- **M** **_arch saw the precious metal

s move largely independently of each other, with silver pushing higher, gold meandering in a narrow range and the PGMs continuing their downward correction before bouncing up once more._** - **W** **_e are expecting gold to run into resistance at $1,480 in the near future, and this is likely to prompt bouts of liquidation and technical selling. A slide towards $1,350 is foreseeable before renewed physical demand cushions the weakness. We still see $1,600 as a target for late in the year on renewed inflationary concerns, despite recent hawkishness from US officials._** - **S** **_ilver has continued to march higher and enters April testing $39 as high gold prices continue to draw investors to silver that might otherwise prefer the yellow metal. Silver’s buoyancy may be seen as an indicator that the gold is expected to show fresh medium term strength. A correction in gold would be likely, however, to push silver into a slide towards $32._** - **P** **_latinum’s early March weakness was driven by Middle Eastern tension and fears over the implications of high oil prices. The tragedy in Japan precipitated a knee-jerk sell-off towards $1,650 although that has now unwound with a bounce towards $1,800. Although in the longer-term the Japanese disaster is unlikely to impinge greatly on platinum demand, the market is watching developments closely and the outlook suggests that platinum prices may struggle to make much headway above $1,800 in the coming weeks._** - **P** **_alladium is in a deficit (unlike the platinum market), but Japan is a larger proportional consumer of palladium than platinum. As a result the price profiles between the two may be similar in the near term, with palladium’s recent bounce unlikely to extend above $800. For the longer term, however, the outlook is much brighter._** The tragedy in Japan has of course been commanding much of the markets’ attention, with the platinum group metals reacting the most strongly, reflecting Japan’s importance to the PGM markets. There is no doubt that demand was curtailed during March and is likely to remain subdued until perhaps June, although a rebound should be expected and we believe that the recent sell-off was an over-reaction - albeit, perhaps, an understandable one. We go into more detail in the Platinum Group Metals chapter of this publication, but continue to expect the prices of both metals to strengthen in the latter part of this year after floundering somewhat during the second and third quarters Part of this, in the professional market at least, may hinge on the fact that there are signs of restlessness from some Federal Reserve officials about the inflationary outlook in the United States, along with the the fact that the European Central Bank is also now expected to raise interest rates, possibly as soon as its April meeting. The statement following the 15th March meeting of the Federal Reserve Open Market Committee (FOMC) noted that the economic recovery had moved on to a firmer footing, with a gradual overall improvement in the labour market. Trading volumes on Comex were marginally higher than in February, but lower than January and substantially below the daily average for 2010. Price ranges in all the major currencies were narrow, with the euro and trade-weighted dollar prices losing on balance, while in US dollar, yen, rupee and renminbi terms, prices eked out small gains. Given the maelstrom of political and economic developments, this performance may seem somewhat surprising. Taken in isolation, for example, the background of near-revolution in parts of the Middle East, growing inflationary fears intensified by rising oil prices and the renewed downgrades of elements of European sovereign debt should, perhaps, be expected to boost gold prices. Markets, however, do not take individual developments in isolation, but reflect the situation as a whole and on the other side of the equation lies the fact that the jewellery market remains diminished, there have been pockets of secondary supply returning to the market and there was also distressed liquidation from Japan in the middle of the month following the tragic developments of the earthquake and the tsunami. |**~~Gold Supply-De~~**

The physical tightness in the market, outlined in our March _One Year Forecast_ , has been reduced to an extent as physical investment activity has fallen away at higher price levels, although it is of interest to note that secondary material in the Middle East is going straight to fabricators as fresh metal is still ha

rd to source. Middle Eastern physical demand is appearing on dips in price, but in comparatively low volume and regional demand overall is still soft.
